title: Hunted in the hills
hook: Mughal armies pursue Banda through the hills for years

segments.voice: Yesterday, a carpenter's bread and fields given to the hands that worked them. Your line was land to the tillers. Did you thank the hands behind a meal? Today the tide turns, and the hunt begins. Day eight hundred forty-three.

Night at Lohgarh. The fort in the hills is surrounded. The emperor's army has come north in force, and the walls won't hold much longer. Inside, tradition says, one Sikh makes an offer. He'll put on Banda Singh's clothes and sit where Banda Singh sits, so that when the enemy breaks in, they'll think they have their man. In the dark, the real Banda Singh slips out through the hills with whoever can follow. By morning the fort has fallen, and the man they capture isn't the one they came for. Today: hunted in the hills.
screen: `LOHGARH IS SURROUNDED.` → `A SIKH WEARS BANDA SINGH'S CLOTHES.` → `OUT INTO THE HILLS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: That night begins a long stretch of Banda Singh's life that has no grand battles to name it. The Mughal armies kept after him, season after season, through the hills and the jungles at the edge of the plains. He'd vanish, regroup, strike, and vanish again. Lands won were lost. Towns changed hands. The people who sheltered his men paid a price. Sikh tellings don't make this part glamorous. It was cold camps, short food, running at night, and the slow grind of being hunted. What kept them going? Sikhs have a phrase for it that appears at the end of the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings: chardi kala. It means something like rising spirits, an ever-ascending spirit. Not cheerfulness. Not pretending things are fine. Chardi kala is the steadiness to keep facing upward when every report is bad. In the Ardas it's paired with a wish for the good of all, which says something about where that spirit is supposed to point. Notice also the man who wore Banda Singh's clothes. Earlier on this path, at Chamkaur, tradition told of a Sikh named Sangat Singh who wore the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away. Now it happens again. That pattern is its own kind of chardi kala: a willingness to stand in someone else's place so the work can keep going. The hills didn't change the hard news. But one borrowed set of clothes bought one night, and one night was enough to keep going.
screen: `A LONG STRETCH WITH NO GRAND BATTLES.` · `VANISH, REGROUP, STRIKE, VANISH.` · `CHARDI KALA: AN EVER-RISING SPIRIT.` · `SOMEONE STANDS IN YOUR PLACE.` · then, large: `KEEP GOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep going through a hard week. Sit, and let the breath come and go on its own. Name, quietly, the thing in your week that feels like being hunted: the deadline, the bill, the worry that keeps finding you. Don't fight it. Just let it be named. Then find one small next step, the size of one night's walk in the hills. Not the whole road. One step. Rest your attention on that step and on your breathing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the phrase chardi kala sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
Hunted in the hills. The long stretch after Lohgarh fell, when Banda Singh and his men were pursued through the hills and jungles and kept going. Today's word.
Your line: keep going. Today, take the one small step you found in the sit, and only that one, and let it count. Day eight hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's years of being pursued through the hills as a time of chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, a phrase that closes the Ardas said at Sikh gatherings.
